studio-river.text: The river begins as snowmelt high in the mountains, where thin streams gather between rocks and run downhill through stands of pine. By the time it reaches the valley it has grown wide and slow, and farmers draw water from it to irrigate fields of wheat, barley and alfalfa. In spring the current carries silt that settles along the banks and enriches the soil; in late summer the level drops and gravel bars appear in the middle of the channel. Towns grew up where the river could be crossed most easily, first by ferry and later by bridges of timber, stone and steel. Today the water also turns the turbines of a small dam, supplies several cities with drinking water, and supports herons, otters and dozens of species of fish. Scientists measure its temperature, flow and chemistry every day, and their records show how the river answers drought, heavy rain and the turning of the seasons.
